note: Born before 34 weeks, so expect a longer follow-up tail: hearing, eyes, and a developmental clinic. Keep those appointments in the log.
Skin-to-skin holding is one of the few things shown to help a very early baby directly. Ask your team how long a session can run.
Late preterm babies look term but tire quickly, jaundice more easily, and feed sleepily — which is exactly why the early weight checks matter.
Feeding, weight gain and diapers run on {name}’s actual age; skills run on corrected age. Both are on this card.
Shorter and more frequent feeds are usual — a preterm baby tires quickly at the breast or the bottle.
Preterm babies often need waking to feed for longer than term babies do. Follow the plan your team gave you rather than a clock.
Ask who is up to date on whooping cough before they hold {them}. Ask your pediatrician about RSV season protection.
Car seat angle and time limits matter more for a preterm baby — many hospitals run a car seat tolerance screen before discharge.
Corrected age is normally used until about age two. After that chronological age takes over and the gap has usually closed.
Reaching a skill later than the chart says is expected — measure from the corrected age, and raise anything that worries you at the next visit.
Changes come with a spray risk. Keep a cloth over {them} while you work.
If {name} was circumcised, follow the aftercare you were given exactly, and call about bleeding, swelling or a fever.
Swollen scrotum and breast tissue from your hormones is common in the first weeks. Your pediatrician checks it at every visit.
Boys average slightly heavier and longer than girls at the same age, which is why the growth charts in Reports use the WHO boys' curves.
Boys reach language milestones a little later on average. The range is wide, and the 18-month screening is the place to raise it.
Wipe front to back at every change.
A little discharge or spotting in the first weeks comes from your hormones and settles on its own. Mention it at the next visit if it worries you.
Only the WHO boys' curves are bundled today, so the growth charts compare {name} against the boys' reference. Your pediatrician's chart is the one to trust.
